items.title: The ministry of the Spirit's spotlight
items.author: J. I. Packer
items.work: Keep in Step with the Spirit (1984)
items.body:
J. I. Packer wrote about the Holy Spirit at a time of much debate about gifts and experiences. Instead of entering only into controversy, he asked a deeper question: what is the central work of the Spirit? His answer became known by an image: the spotlight ministry.

## Illuminate another

Packer recalls what Jesus said about the Spirit: "He will glorify me" (John 16:14). A well-positioned spotlight illuminates a building at night, and no one looks at the lamp. That's how the Spirit is: it doesn't draw attention to itself, but points to Christ. Where Christ is exalted, known, and loved, there the Spirit is at work.

## Holiness, not just experience

For Packer, the greatest sign of the Spirit's presence is not the intensity of emotions nor the spectacular nature of the gifts, but holiness: the fruit of the Spirit described in Galatians 5, as love, joy, peace, patience, and self-control. He does not despise experiences; He only puts them in the right place. An experience that no longer produces love for Christ and more obedience must be examined.

## Walking in rhythm

The original title talks about keeping pace with the Spirit (Galatians 5:25). Packer describes the Christian life as a walk in which we follow the Spirit's guidance through the Word, prayer, and church fellowship. It is not passivity or activism, but humble cooperation: the Spirit works in us, and we work our salvation with fear and trembling (Philippians 2:12–13).

## A simple test

Packer leaves a useful criterion for evaluating movements, worship, and experiences: Is Christ being magnified? Do people leave loving Jesus, His Word, and His people more? If so, the spotlight is on in the right place.

items.title: The Spirit that unites us to Christ
items.author: Sinclair Ferguson
items.work: The Holy Spirit (1996)
items.body:
Sinclair Ferguson, a Scottish theologian, wrote one of the most comprehensive and pastoral studies on the Holy Spirit in the Reformed tradition. A central theme runs through the book: the main work of the Spirit in salvation is to unite us to Christ.

## Christ outside of us, Christ within us

Calvin said that while Christ remains outside of us, everything He suffered and did for our salvation is useless to us. Ferguson develops this idea: the Spirit is the bond that unites us to Christ. Through faith, which is the gift of the Spirit, we receive everything that is in Christ: justification, adoption, sanctification, and the hope of glory.

## The Spirit in the life of Jesus

A beautiful contribution of the book is to show the Spirit working in Jesus' own life: in the conception, baptism, temptations in the desert, miracles, the cross, and resurrection. The same Spirit that led Jesus in all his work is given to the church. That is why the Christian life is a life shaped in the image of the Son.

## A real sanctification

Ferguson insists that sanctification is not a moral effort apart from grace. United to Christ, we die with him to sin and rise with him to new life (Romans 6). The Spirit applies this reality day after day. We fight against sin not to achieve union with Christ, but because we are already united to him.

## For everyday use

The doctrine of union with Christ brings deep comfort: everything that belongs to Christ is yours, and you belong to Him. In times of weakness, remember: you are not just trying to imitate Jesus from afar; His Spirit lives in you and binds you to Him forever.

items.title: The work of the Holy Spirit
items.author: Abraham Kuyper
items.work: The Work of the Holy Spirit (Het werk van den Heiligen Geest, 1888)
items.body:
Abraham Kuyper was a theologian, journalist, university founder, and prime minister of the Netherlands. Even with an intense political agenda, he wrote one of the most comprehensive treatises on the Holy Spirit in the Reformed tradition. Kuyper wanted to correct an oversight: many churches spoke of the Father and the Son, but almost nothing of the Spirit.

## The Spirit in creation

Kuyper begins before salvation. The Spirit hovered over the waters in creation (Genesis 1:2). He gives life, order, and beauty to the world. Kuyper attributes to the Spirit even the natural gifts: the skill of the craftsman, the talent of the artist, the wisdom of the ruler. Bezalel, who built the tabernacle, was filled with the Spirit to work with art (Exodus 31). This means that no honest work is outside God's interest.

## The Spirit in redemption

Then, Kuyper describes the work of the Spirit in salvation: he inspired the Scriptures, formed the body of Christ in Mary's womb, anointed Jesus in his ministry, regenerates sinners, produces faith, unites the believer to Christ, and sanctifies him. Everything Christ has gained, the Spirit applies.

## The Spirit in the church and in the individual

Kuyper balances the communal and personal dimensions. The Spirit dwells in the church as a temple and also in every believer. He distributes gifts for the edification of all and produces fruits of love and holiness. A spirituality that despises the church or ignores the heart is incomplete.

## To live

Kuyper's work broadens the perspective: the Spirit is present in worship and also in Monday work. Ask him not only for strength to pray, but for wisdom to work, creativity to serve, and love to live together. Every area of life is territory where the Spirit wants to act.

items.title: Hope in times of fear
items.author: Tim Keller
items.work: Hope in Times of Fear (2021)
items.body:
Tim Keller wrote Hope in Times of Fear during the pandemic while treating the cancer that would lead to his death in 2023. The theme is the resurrection of Jesus and what it means for those living in a world marked by fear and uncertainty. It is not a theoretical book: it is the hope of someone who looked at their own death.

## The resurrection happened

Keller begins with the fact. The Christian faith does not rely on an abstract teaching, but on a historical event: the empty tomb and Jesus' appearances to many witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). He reminds us that if the resurrection did not happen, Christianity falls, as Paul himself admits. But if it did, everything changes.

## A hope that looks ahead

The resurrection of Jesus is the firstfruits of the harvest. It guarantees that those who are in it will also rise again. Keller insists that Christian hope is not to flee the world to a vacant heaven, but to wait for the renewal of all things: resurrected bodies, a new creation, full righteousness, and the presence of God among His people (Revelation 21).

## Fear and courage

Because of this, the Christian can face fear differently. Not denying pain, but knowing that death does not have the final word. Keller notes that the hope of resurrection has produced, throughout history, courageous Christians in caring for the sick, in the struggle for justice, and in faithfulness under persecution.

## To live today

Keller, in his last months of life, publicly said that illness had led him to believe in the resurrection in a more personal and real way than before. The book's invitation is the same: to let the resurrection cease to be just doctrine and become the hope that sustains today.

items.title: The sky, a world of love
items.author: Jonathan Edwards
items.work: Charity and Its Fruits, final sermon "Heaven Is a World of Love" (1738)
items.body:
Jonathan Edwards, pastor and theologian from New England, considered one of the greatest thinkers in American history, preached in 1738 a series of sermons on 1 Corinthians 13. The last of them has an unforgettable title: heaven is a world of love.

## Where love is perfect

Edwards starts from Paul's statement that love never ends (1 Corinthians 13:8). Faith will give way to vision, and hope to possession. But love remains and reaches perfection. That is why heaven can be described as the place where love is full: God's love poured out without limits and the love of the saints for one another, without envy, without pride, and without fear of losing.

## The Source of Love

For Edwards, heaven is not beautiful because of golden streets, but because God is there, who is love. The Father, the Son, and the Spirit live in eternal communion, and the redeemed are brought into that love. Each one loves and is loved according to their ability, and all are satisfied, because no one desires what they do not have.

## A love that grows

Edwards suggests something surprising: the joy of heaven will not be static. Since God is infinite, there will always be more to know and love. Eternity will not be boredom, but endless discovery.

## Living there already

The sermon ends with an appeal. If heaven is a world of love, whoever intends to get there must learn to love now. Edwards says that the Christian life is a journey toward that world, and that every act of true love is a taste of the homeland. Hell, by contrast, is a world without love. The question, then, is personal: is your heart being prepared for the place where only love dwells?

items.title: The pilgrim crosses the river
items.author: John Bunyan
items.work: The Pilgrim's Progress (1678)
items.body:
John Bunyan was a poor tinsmith and Baptist preacher who spent twelve years imprisoned for preaching without a license. In prison, he wrote an allegory that became one of the most read books in history after the Bible: The Pilgrim. A Christian, the main character, leaves the City of Destruction and walks to the Heavenly City. The final scene is one of the most moving in Christian literature.

## A path full of trials

Before the end, the pilgrim passes through the Swamp of Discouragement, the Hill of Difficulty, the Valley of Humiliation, the Vanity Fair, and the Castle of Doubt. Bunyan portrays Christian life with realism: there are falls, temptations, and discouragements, but there are also faithful companions, shelter, and the cross, where the burden of guilt falls from the Christian's shoulders.

## The river without a bridge

Upon approaching the Heavenly City, the pilgrim finds a deep river, without a bridge. It is the image of death. Christian is afraid and almost drowns, overwhelmed by memories of his sins. His companion, Hopeful, holds him and says he feels the depths, and that the depths are good. Then Christians remember Christ and the promise of Isaiah 43:2: when you pass through the waters, I will be with you. And cross over.

## On the other side

On the other side, angels welcome the pilgrims, and they enter the city to the sound of trumpets. Bunyan describes the joy of those who arrive home. Death, for the believer, is not the end of the road, but the last crossing before glory.

## For our trip

The Pilgrim reminds us that we are strangers in this world, on the way to the homeland. It is worth asking: on what stretch of the path am I? And it is worth resting in the certainty of Hope: the riverbed is firm for those who are in Christ.

items.title: Sex as renewal of the alliance
items.author: Tim Keller
items.work: The Meaning of Marriage (2011), chapter on sexuality
items.body:
In the book The Meaning of Marriage, Tim Keller dedicates an entire chapter to sex. He notes that the modern world treats sex as an appetite to be satisfied or as a form of personal expression, and that the Christian view is at once higher and more demanding.

## More than a pleasure

Keller begins by stating that the Bible is not against sex. It celebrates it, as seen in Song of Songs. Sex is good because it was created by God. But precisely because it is so powerful, it was given with a purpose: to unite two people entirely, body and soul, within a covenant.

## Renew the promise

Keller's most well-known image is that sex is an act of renewing the covenant. In marriage, husband and wife made a public promise to belong to each other for life. In sexual relations, they say with the body what they promised with their mouth: "I am all yours, forever." Outside of marriage, the body says something that life is not saying. That is why the Bible reserves sex for marriage between a man and a woman.

## Why wait

Keller responds to common objections: "but we love each other" or "we need to know if we match." He argues that sex before commitment tends to create false intimacy, without the security of promise, and ends up teaching the person to protect themselves rather than surrender. Waiting is not repression; it is preparation for a complete surrender.

## Grace for those who have already made mistakes

Keller also speaks to those who have lived differently. The gospel is not a court with no way out. In Christ there is complete forgiveness and a real new beginning. Purity is not just an untouched past, but a path that can be chosen today, by grace.

items.title: Sex and the supremacy of Christ
items.author: John Piper
items.work: Sex and the Supremacy of Christ (org. com Justin Taylor, 2005)
items.body:
John Piper and Justin Taylor organized a book with lectures by various pastors on sexuality. The title sums up Piper's thesis: sex, like everything in life, exists for the glory of Christ. When Christ is the greatest treasure, sex finds its right place.

## God made sex to reveal something

Piper argues that God created sexuality to teach us about it. The union of marriage is an image of the union between Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Conjugal fidelity shows the fidelity of Christ. Therefore, when sex is used outside God's design, He tells a lie about the gospel itself.

## Why purity is a struggle

Piper is realistic: sexual temptation is strong, especially in a world saturated with images. He does not offer tricks, but a strategy of faith. Sexual sin promises pleasure; the answer is not just to say "no," but to find greater pleasure in God. It is the logic he calls Christian hedonism: we fight against false pleasures with the promise of higher joys.

## Practical weapons

Among the advice Piper often gives are: avoid occasions, as Paul commands (1 Corinthians 6:18); fill your mind with God's promises; confess sin to trusted brothers; and cultivate healthy relationships. He also insists that Christian lovers set clear boundaries before passion decides for them.

## Hope, not despair

For those who have already fallen, Piper reminds us that the cross is enough. Guilt doesn't have to be the last word. The same Christ who forgives is what gives strength to start over. Purity is the fruit of grace, not a trophy for those who never erred.

items.title: The unpopular virtue
items.author: C. S. Lewis (com uma leitura reformada)
items.work: Pure and Simple Christianity (Mere Christianity, 1952), chapter on sexual morality
items.body:
C. S. Lewis was not reformed. He was Anglican, a literature professor at Oxford and Cambridge, and author of The Chronicles of Narnia. But his chapter on sexual morality in Pure and Simple Christianity is cited by Christians of many traditions, including Reformed, for the clarity with which it addresses the subject.

## The Christian rule

Lewis sums up Christian ethics directly: either marriage, with complete fidelity to the spouse, or total abstinence. He admits that this rule is so difficult and so contrary to our instincts that either Christianity is wrong, or our sexual instinct is disordered. And he concludes that it is instinct that has deviated.

## Excessive appetite

To illustrate, Lewis makes a famous comparison. Imagine a country where people fill theaters to see someone slowly lift the lid of a plate, showing a piece of meat. We would say something went wrong with that people's appetite. Similarly, the modern obsession with sex shows that desire has been distorted. It is not saying that sex is bad, but that it has become disproportionate.

## It's not the worst sin

Lewis makes an important observation: the sins of the flesh are serious, but not the worst. Pride, cruelty, and a cold spirit of judgment can be more dangerous. This protects against a hypocritical morality that condemns others and ignores one's own heart.

## The reformed reading

The Reformed tradition agrees with Lewis on the standard and adds emphasis on grace: we do not attain chastity only through effort, but through the work of the Spirit in those united to Christ. Lewis himself ends by saying that when we fall, we must get up and start over, asking God for help. Purity is a path of continuous repentance and hope.

items.title: What happened to the human race?
items.author: Francis Schaeffer e C. Everett Koop
items.work: Whatever Happened to the Human Race? (1979)
items.body:
Francis Schaeffer was a Presbyterian pastor and thinker who founded the L'Abri community in Switzerland, where young people from all over the world came to discuss faith and culture. In 1979, he joined Dr. C. Everett Koop, a pediatric surgeon who would later become head of public health in the United States, to write a book and produce a series of films about the value of human life.

## A prophetic warning

Schaeffer and Koop realized that the acceptance of abortion was not an isolated fact. It revealed a profound change in how society viewed the human being. If life comes to count according to the usefulness, health, or desires of others, then no one is safe: neither the baby in the womb, nor the elderly, nor the person with a disability. They warned that the same logic would lead to infanticide and euthanasia.

## The image of God

The basis of the argument is biblical. The human being has value because he was created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), not because he produces, decides, or is desired. Psalm 139 describes God forming the person in the womb. Human life does not begin to have dignity when someone recognizes it; it already has it, because God gave it.

## Science confirms

Koop, as a doctor, brought the perspective of medicine: from conception there is a distinct human being, with their own genetic code, in development. It is not a part of the mother's body, but another life that depends on her.

## More than just protesting

Schaeffer insisted that Christians should not only condemn, but act with compassion: support pregnant women in difficulty, take in children, care for the vulnerable, and offer women who have aborted the grace and forgiveness of Christ. Defending life is also serving life.

items.title: Abortion: a rational look at an emotional issue
items.author: R. C. Sproul
items.work: Abortion: A Rational Look at an Emotional Issue (1990)
items.body:
R. C. Sproul knew that few topics arouse as much emotion as abortion. That is why he wrote a book with a clear proposal: to think calmly, in the light of the Bible and reason, without shouting and without slogans.

## The decisive question

Sproul shows that the entire debate depends on one question: is what is in the womb a human life? If it is not, abortion would be a matter of personal choice. But if it is, no personal choice justifies taking an innocent life. He argues that both the Bible and biology point to the same answer: it is about a human being in development.

## When in doubt, protect

Sproul adds an argument of caution. Even those who say they don't know when life begins should act cautiously. If a hunter hears a noise in the bush and doesn't know if it's an animal or a person, he doesn't shoot. Uncertainty asks for protection, not permission.

## Arguments examined

The book addresses frequent objections, such as autonomy over one's own body, difficult cases of violence, and the idea that anti-abortion laws impose a religion. Sproul treats each with respect, but concludes that defending life is a matter of justice for the most vulnerable, not just of particular faith.

## Compassion and responsibility

Sproul insists that the church has the duty to care for women in difficult situations, offering concrete help before and after childbirth. And he reminds us that Christ's forgiveness reaches those who have already had an abortion. The defense of life and the offering of grace go hand in hand.

items.title: Formed in the womb: life and grace
items.author: John Piper
items.work: Sermons and articles on the holiness of life (Desiring God)
items.body:
John Piper preached and wrote many times about abortion throughout his ministry in Minneapolis. He always united two things that rarely go hand in hand in public debate: a firm defense of life and a deep tenderness for those hurt by this reality.

## What the Bible says about the womb

Piper often starts from texts like Psalm 139:13–16, where the psalmist says God wove him in the womb of the mother, and Jeremiah 1:5, where God claims to have known the prophet before forming him. He also recalls that John the Baptist leapt for joy in Elizabeth's womb upon hearing Mary's greeting (Luke 1:41). For Piper, the Bible treats the child in the womb as a person before God.

## A matter of justice

Piper argues that abortion is not just a private decision, but a matter of justice, because it involves taking the life of someone who cannot defend themselves. He calls Christians to speak courageously on behalf of the vulnerable, as the Bible commands in Proverbs 31:8.

## Grace for the wounded

At the same time, Piper speaks very carefully to the women and men who have participated in an abortion. He says there is no sin too great for the blood of Christ. Forgiveness is complete, and guilt can be taken to the cross. Churches should be places of healing, not shame.

## Concrete action

Piper encourages the church to support centers for pregnant women, to consider adoption and foster care, and to care for single mothers. Defending life costs time, money, and love. But this is how the church shows that the gospel values every person.

items.title: When sinners say yes
items.author: Dave Harvey
items.work: When Sinners Say "I Do" (2007)
items.body:
Dave Harvey, pastor and author linked to the Sovereign Grace movement, wrote a book about marriage with a realistic premise: every marriage unites two sinners. Instead of hiding this, he proposes that the couple learn to live the gospel precisely there.

## Theology matters in marriage

Harvey begins by saying that what we believe about God and sin shapes how we treat our spouse. Those who think the biggest problem in marriage is the other will always be demanding. Those who recognize their own sin begin to be more humble, patient, and quick to ask for forgiveness.

## The worst sinner I know

One phrase marks the book: Harvey invites each spouse to consider themselves the worst sinner they know, following Paul's example (1 Timothy 1:15). This changes everything in a discussion. Instead of starting by pointing out the other's mistake, each begins by examining their own heart.

## Mercy every day

Harvey insists that marriage needs daily mercy: forgiving without holding score, not bringing back old offenses, covering small flaws with love (1 Peter 4:8). At the same time, he teaches to confront with meekness when necessary, always seeking to restore, not to win.

## Practical advice

Among the book's guidelines are: to confess specifically and quickly, without excuses; to forgive as God forgave us in Christ; to serve before expecting to be served; and to remember that earthly marriage points to something greater, the marriage of Christ with His church. Sinners who say yes can, by grace, build a home full of hope.

items.title: Sacred marriage: more saints than happy
items.author: Gary Thomas (com uma leitura reformada)
items.work: Sacred Marriage (2000)
items.body:
Gary Thomas is an evangelical author whose book Sacred Marriage became well known for a provocative question: what if God planned marriage more to make us saints than to make us happy? The question resonates with the Reformed tradition, which has always seen lifelong as the stage for sanctification.

## The school of holiness

Thomas shows that marriage reveals who we really are. Selfishness, impatience, and pride appear when we share life with someone every day. Instead of seeing this as proof that marriage has failed, he proposes seeing it as opportunity: God uses the spouse to mold us into the image of Christ.

## Learning to love

The book deals with love as a spiritual discipline. Loving when it is easy does not require much. But loving when the other disappoints, when routine weighs on us, or when illness arrives, forms in us the character of Christ, who loved the church unconditionally (Ephesians 5:25).

## Prayer and forgiveness

Thomas reminds us that marriage teaches us to pray and to forgive. Many couples discover their own dependence on God precisely in crises. Praying together, praying for the spouse, and confessing sins to each other are practices that strengthen unity and the heart.

## Recast reading

The Reformed tradition agrees with Thomas's thesis and adds that happiness is not despised: it is the fruit of a life centered on God. Marriage is not our god, but a gift to lead us to God. When we first seek the Kingdom, many joys come with it.

items.title: Advice for a marriage that lasts
items.author: Hernandes Dias Lopes
items.work: A frequent theme in his sermons and books about family
items.body:
Hernandes Dias Lopes, a Brazilian Presbyterian pastor, frequently preaches and writes about family and marriage. His messages often combine biblical exposition and practical advice for couples. This article brings together, in our own words, the pillars of this teaching.

## Marriage begins in God

In Hernandes' reading, marriage is not a human invention nor a contract that dissolves when feelings diminish. It was instituted by God in Eden (Genesis 2:24) and confirmed by Jesus. Therefore, the first advice is to put God at the center: a couple who pray, read the Bible, and attend church together has a solid foundation to face crises.

## To leave, unite, and become one

The text of Genesis 2:24 is often explained in three verbs. Leaving father and mother: the new home needs autonomy and priority. Uniting: the commitment is loyalty and exclusivity. Becoming one flesh: the union is total, involving body, soul, dreams, and finances.

## Daily care

Among the practical advice that appears in sermons on the subject are: talk every day and listen carefully; never let the sun set on anger (Ephesians 4:26); praise more than criticize; manage finances with transparency; protect the marriage from vices and infidelity, including virtual infidelity; and cultivate romance even after many years.

## When the crisis arrives

Every marriage passes through deserts. The path is not to give up, but to seek God, ask for forgiveness, forgive, and seek pastoral help when necessary. The love God asks for is the love of 1 Corinthians 13: patient, kind, bearable of all things. And this love is possible because it is born from Christ's love for us.

items.title: Planting churches where Christ is not yet known
items.author: Ronaldo Lidório
items.work: Ministry and writings on church planting and missionary anthropology
items.body:
Ronaldo Lidório is a Presbyterian pastor, missionary, and Brazilian anthropologist. He spent years among the Konkombas, in northern Ghana, and later served with indigenous peoples of the Amazon. From his experience in the field and study was born a conviction he repeats insistently: mission is not just about carrying a message, it is about seeing a church born, grow, and remain among a people.

## Listen before you speak

Lidório reminds us that the gospel is always the same, but it reaches people who think, feel, and decide within a culture. That's why the missionary needs to learn the language, proverbs, beliefs, and fears of that people. Not to change the message, but so that it is truly understood. Those who skip this stage usually reap superficial conversions or a faith mixed with old beliefs.

## Fidelity without syncretism

To contextualize is not to negotiate the truth. Scripture judges every culture, including that of the missionary. The goal is for Christ to be confessed with the words of that people, without the gospel losing the cross, repentance, and grace. Lidório insists on the translation of the Bible and the teaching of the Word as the path for a church that thinks biblically for itself.

## A church that multiplies

The goal is not to create dependence on the missionary, but to train local leaders. A church planted with health prays, reads the Bible, cares for its own, and sends others. When the missionary leaves, the work continues, because they belong to Christ and to that people.

## For the Brazilian church

Brazil has become a country that sends missionaries. This is a reason for gratitude and responsibility: to pray for those in the fields, to sustain with fidelity, to prepare well those who go, and to remember that there are still thousands of peoples without a church among them.

Paul asks: how will they listen if there is no one to preach? God's answer remains sent people, with the Bible open and a heart willing to learn.

items.title: What the persecuted church teaches us
items.author: Nik Ripken
items.work: The Insanity of God (2013)
items.body:
Nik Ripken is the name used by an American Baptist missionary who served for years in Somalia, amid war and famine. There he saw brothers being killed because of faith and even wondered if the gospel could survive in places like this. The answer came from extensive research: he interviewed hundreds of Christians who had lived under persecution in various countries.

## Persecution is no exception

Ripken realized that, for much of the church in the world, suffering for Christ is normal. The persecuted brothers did not see themselves as heroes, but as disciples who took Jesus' words seriously: if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. For them, the question was not how to avoid suffering, but how to be faithful within it.

## The fear that harms the most

One of the harshest lessons is that often the biggest obstacle is not the persecutor, but the fear of the Christians themselves. Those who remain silent about Jesus to protect themselves end up leaving their neighbors unheard. The persecuted believers say that the church grew precisely when they decided to speak out, even at the price.

## Memory, prayer, and Scripture

In places where the Bible is forbidden, it is decorated, sung, and copied by hand. Ripken heard stories of brothers who, in prison, sustained themselves with verses and hymns kept in their hearts. This confronts the free church, which has Bibles at home and little time for them.

## How to answer from here

Hebrews commands us to remember the prisoners as if we were imprisoned with them. We can pray with names and countries, inform the church, support serious ministries that serve the persecuted, and above all, learn from them the courage to speak of Christ where we are.

The cross was not the end of Jesus' story, and persecution is not the end of the church. The Lord continues to build up His people, and the gates of hell will not prevail.

items.title: The new map of Christianity
items.author: Philip Jenkins (com uma leitura reformada)
items.work: The Next Christendom (2002)
items.body:
For centuries, when people spoke of Christianity, people thought of Europe and North America. Historian Philip Jenkins showed that this picture is behind us. The center of gravity of the Christian faith shifted to the Global South: Africa, Latin America, and parts of Asia. Today, the typical Christian is more likely to be a Nigerian woman or a young Brazilian than a European.

## A faith that grows among the poor

Jenkins notes that the church grows stronger in places of poverty, instability, and persecution. There the Bible is read urgently: stories of exile, famine, healing, and deliverance sound like daily news. This returns to the entire church a more concrete reading of the Scriptures.

## Mission in all directions

The mission map has also changed. Churches in Korea, Brazil, Nigeria, and many other countries send missionaries, including to secularized Europe. Mission is no longer a one-way street from North to South. Now it is from everywhere to everywhere, as it has always been God's purpose.

## A revised reading

Jenkins describes trends as a historian, not as a theologian. Numerical growth does not guarantee fidelity. In many regions, the most advanced Christianity mixes the gospel with promises of prosperity or traditional religious practices. That is why the greatest challenge for the Southern church is formation: good pastors, good theology, catechisms, and translated Bibles. Seminaries and Reformed churches have much to offer here, with humility to also learn.

## What this asks of us

It asks for gratitude, because God is gathering a people of every tribe and language, as Revelation 7 describes. It asks for commitment to sound doctrine and to the preparation of leaders. And it asks that the Brazilian church joyfully assume its place in this history: to receive, send, and serve.

items.title: Loving as Christ loves: the opposite of violence
items.author: Hernandes Dias Lopes
items.work: Expository commentary on Ephesians (Hagnos)
items.body:
Hernandes Dias Lopes, a Presbyterian pastor and one of Brazil's best-known exhibition preachers, dedicated many pages to Ephesians 5, the text that speaks of marriage in the light of Christ and the church. A careful reading of this chapter dismantles any attempt to use the Bible to justify violence within the home.

## The pattern is the cross

Paul does not command the husband to command. He commands the husband to love, and love as Christ loved the church and gave himself for it. The model of leadership in the home is a man who gives his life, not a man who takes the life of his wife with shouting, threats, control, or aggression. Whoever hurts the woman is not exercising the authority God gave; they are denying Christ Himself who says He follows.

## Taking care of your own body

The apostle adds that the husband must love his wife as his own body, feeding and caring for her. No one in good conscience beats their own body. The image is one of protection, tenderness, and sustenance. Hernandes insists that Christian marriage is a covenant of love, not a relationship of possession.

## Submission is not subjection to violence

The wife is called to respect her husband in the Lord, and that never means obeying sin nor enduring abuse in silence. Biblical submission happens under Christ, and Christ does not command anyone to accept aggression. When the home becomes a place of violence, the woman has the right to seek protection, and the church has the duty to support her and confront the aggressor.

## A call to men

The text ends with an appeal: husbands, look at the cross. True repentance begins with the recognition of sin, without excuses and without blaming the victim, and continues with responsibility before the church and the law. The gospel forgives the repentant sinner but does not cover up sin.

The Christian home must be the safest place in the world, because there lives a man who learned to love with Jesus.

items.title: Until when? The church in the face of violence against women
items.author: Sérgio Andrade (com uma leitura reformada)
items.work: Until when? Violence against women (Diakonia / World Evangelical Alliance)
items.body:
Pastor Sérgio Andrade, who coordinated counseling and pastoral care work at the Diaconia, wrote a short and strong text with a question in the title: until when? He starts from a painful observation: violence against women in Brazil is not hidden. It happens at home, on the street, at work, and in public spaces, and often everyone knows it.

## A learned violence

Andrade reminds us that this violence is not only physical. It includes threats, humiliation, control, sexual abuse, and deprivation of freedom. And it is taught: boys grow up hearing that they are superior and have the right to control a woman's life. Therefore, change needs to start early, in the education of children.

## Silence also hurts

One of the most serious points of the text is the criticism of what it calls false pacification: advising women to remain silent to maintain appearances. This silence, even when well-intentioned, protects the aggressor and prolongs suffering. The church cannot cover up or relativize abuse.

## Jesus and the women

Andrade points to the Gospels. Jesus talks with the Samaritan woman when this was frowned upon, honors his own mother, heals and restores dignity to the woman who had suffered for twelve years, and welcomes women among those who followed him. The Lord never treated the woman as property.

## A revised reading

The Reformed tradition teaches that man and woman have the same dignity as the image of God, and that the husband's leadership is called to sacrificial service, never license to dominate. Even those who disagree with some of the author's emphases may receive his central appeal.

## What the church can do

Teaching the Bible without justifying domination, preparing pastors and leaders to welcome, helping victims overcome fear and shame, and calling aggressors to repentance and responsibility. The question remains true for each community: until when?

items.title: It's not your fault: hope for those who suffer violence
items.author: Justin e Lindsey Holcomb
items.work: Is It My Fault? Hope and Healing for Those Suffering Domestic Violence (2014)
items.body:
Justin Holcomb, pastor and theology professor, and his wife Lindsey, who has worked with victims of violence, wrote a book with a question that many Christian women silently ask: is it my fault? Their answer, based on Scripture, is clear: no. Violence is the sin of those who practice it.

## God sees and cares

The Psalms say that the Lord hates violence and that he who loves violence hates. God is not indifferent to the crying of someone hurt inside the house. The Holcombs remind us that the victim does not need to prove they deserve protection: they are the image of God, and that is enough.

## Acknowledge abuse

The book helps to name what happens. Abuse is not just slaps or punches. It is also controlling money, isolating from family, watching the phone, threatening, humiliating, forcing relationships, and making the person feel like they are going crazy. When this pattern repeats, it is not a couple's fight: it is violence.

## Safety first

The authors insist that protecting life comes before any other decision. Seeking help, leaving home for a while, going to the police and justice are not lack of faith. In Brazil, the Women's Hotline calls 180, and in emergencies the number is 190.

## The role of the church

The church must listen, believe, protect, and walk together, without pressing for hasty reconciliation. Forgiveness is not the same as living again under risk. With the aggressor, the path is confrontation, discipline, and responsibility, and only real and demonstrated repentance over time can open another conversation.

## Hope in Christ

Jesus was wounded, humiliated, and understands the pain of those who suffer. In Him there is healing for shame and hope to rebuild life. If you are going through this, seek help today: you are not alone.

items.title: Free from all, servant of all
items.author: Martinho Lutero
items.work: On Christian Liberty (Von der Freiheit eines Christenmenschen, 1520)
items.body:
In 1520, at the height of tension with Rome, Martin Luther wrote a small treatise that became one of the most beloved texts of the Reformation. He starts from a paradox: the Christian is the free master of all things and is subject to no one; and the Christian is a servant to all and subject to all. Both phrases are true at the same time, and only the gospel explains how.

## Free by faith

For Luther, no external work makes the soul righteous before God. Fasting, pilgrimages, and rites do not reach the heart. What justifies is the Word of God received by faith. When we believe in the promise, Christ and all that belongs to him become ours. The conscience, once accused, finds rest, because the righteousness that covers us is not ours.

## The happy exchange

Luther describes union with Christ as a marriage. The poor and sinful bride receives the riches of the bridegroom, and the bridegroom takes upon himself the bride's debts. Our sin, our death, and our condemnation go to Christ; His righteousness, life, and salvation come to us. This exchange is not a reward for the best, but a gift for those who have nothing.

## Servants for love

Precisely because he is free, the Christian becomes a servant. He no longer does good works to be accepted, and so he can do them freely, thinking of the good of others. Luther says we must be to one another as Christ was to us. Faith receives everything from God; love gives everything to our neighbor.

## Neither pride nor neglect

This teaching cuts through two evils. It cuts the pride of those who think they buy God's favor, and they cut the laziness of those who think grace dispenses with love. Christian freedom is not license, it is joy that overflows in service.

This week, do a good work in secret, without expecting return, just because you have already been loved in Christ. Before you start, give thanks: what you do doesn't pay for anything, it only answers to those who paid for everything.

items.title: Neither legalism nor libertinism: the whole Christ
items.author: Sinclair Ferguson
items.work: The Whole Christ (2016)
items.body:
Sinclair Ferguson, a Scottish pastor and theology professor, wrote a book that starts from an ancient controversy in eighteenth-century Scotland, known as the Marrow controversy. The discussion seems distant, but it touches on a question every Christian faces: how do grace, law, and the certainty of salvation relate?

## Two deviations with the same root

Ferguson shows that legalism and antinomianism, which is the rejection of the law in the Christian life, seem opposed, but they arise from the same place. Both separate the benefits of Christ from the person of Christ. The legalist wants the blessing, but thinks he needs to pay for it. The antinomian wants forgiveness, but does not want the Lord who offers it. In both, God is seen as a suspicious patron, not as a generous Father.

## Christ before the benefits

The remedy is to receive Christ Himself, whole, freely offered in the gospel. In Him we have justification and sanctification, forgiveness and new life, without one thing separating from the other. No one needs to first become good enough to come to Him. The invitation is for sinners as sinners.

## The law in the right place

Ferguson reminds us that the law is not the enemy of the believer. It does not save us, but it reveals the character of God and describes the life of love that the Spirit produces. Those who have been reached by grace begin to love what they once feared. Obedience ceases to be a price and becomes gratitude.

## Certainty that it is born from the gospel

Many believers live insecure because they look too much at themselves. Ferguson points outward: certainty is born from contemplating God's grace in Christ and His promises. The fruits confirm, but the foundation is the Savior.

Today, if you catch yourself thinking that God only accepts you when you are well, stop and read Titus 2 slowly. There, the same grace that saves also educates. Receive Christ again, whole, and obey as a child, not as an employee.

items.title: The God who truly reigns
items.author: A. W. Pink
items.work: The Sovereignty of God (1918)
items.body:
Arthur W. Pink was an English pastor and writer who spent much of his life away from the spotlight, writing Bible studies for a small group of readers. One of his books, however, survived the century and is still read worldwide: a passionate defense that God is, in fact, God.

## A God who is not a hostage

Pink was troubled by a common idea in his time: that of a well-intentioned but weak God who desires many things and depends on human goodwill to accomplish them. For him, this is not the God of the Bible. The Lord of the Scriptures does everything that pleases Him, in heaven and on earth. Nothing catches Him by surprise, nothing defeats Him, nothing escapes His rule.

## Sovereignty in creation and salvation

The book passes through nature, history, angels, and men, and reaches salvation. Pink shows that grace is not an offering God leaves on the table hoping someone will be interested. It is God Himself who chooses, calls, regenerates, and keeps His own. This does not nullify human responsibility, but it takes away from us the merit.

## A consolation, not a puzzle

Pink insisted that this doctrine was not given to fuel cold discussions. It humbles pride because it shows that we depend on God in everything. And it comforts the afflicted, because it assures that even pain is in the hands of a wise Father. As Nebuchadnezzar learned, no one can stop God's hand or ask Him: what are you doing?

## Worship as a response

Pink's conclusion is practical: a sovereign God deserves to be feared, obeyed, and worshipped. Prayer gains strength because we speak to those who can act. Obedience gains joy because we serve those who do not fail.

Read Daniel 4 this week. Then, write a concern that has kept you awake at night and, next to it, the phrase: the Most High has dominion. Pray to hand this situation over to Him, with trust and reverence.

items.title: Trusting when we don't understand
items.author: Jerry Bridges
items.work: Trusting God (1988)
items.body:
Jerry Bridges served for decades in the missionary organization Navegantes and became known for writing about the Christian life with simplicity and depth. In one of his most widely read books, he addresses a question every believer faces sooner or later: how to trust God when life hurts?

## Three truths that sustain

Bridges sums up the path in three biblical statements. God is completely sovereign: nothing happens outside His control. God is infinite in wisdom: He knows what is best, even when we don't. And God is perfect in love: everything He does with His own is born from His care. If one of these three truths falls, trust collapses. Together, they sustain us.

## Trusting is not understanding everything

One of the strongest lessons from the book is that trust does not depend on explanation. Often we will not know why something happened. Bridges does not promise answers for every tear. He points to the character of God revealed in Scripture. We may not understand God's hand, but we can trust His heart.

## Providence in the details

The author shows that God's sovereignty is not only about big events. It reaches the small things: a diagnosis, a lost job, a decision by another person that affects us. Even the wrong actions of others do not escape God's government, who is able to turn them into good for those who love Him, as He did with Joseph.

## A daily choice

Bridges reminds us that trusting is also a decision. In dark times, we choose to believe what God said, not what fear suggests. This choice is nourished by the Word, prayer, and the memory of past faithfulness.

Choose a verse from Romans 8 today and repeat it throughout the day, especially when anxiety is tight. Tell God sincerely: I don't understand, but I trust in you. This simple prayer is also faith.

items.title: Learning to pray with the apostle Paul
items.author: D. A. Carson
items.work: A Call to Spiritual Reformation (1992)
items.body:
Don Carson, a New Testament scholar, noticed that many churches talk a lot about prayer but pray little and poorly. His proposal was simple and profound: if we want to renew our prayer life, we need to learn from the prayers God recorded in the Bible, especially those of the apostle Paul.

## Pray for what matters

As he studies Paul's prayers, Carson notices something that confronts us. Paul rarely prays for health, finances, or circumstances, although these things are not forbidden. He prays that the brothers may know God better, grow in love, understand the hope of the calling, and live in a way worthy of the Lord. Our request lists are usually quite different.

## Plan to pray

Carson says that prayer does not happen by chance. Those who expect to want to pray rarely pray. That's why he recommends planning: set aside some time, use lists, pray quietly or aloud so as not to get distracted, and mix worship, confession, gratitude, and requests. Discipline does not kill spontaneity; it opens space for fellowship to grow.

## Gratitude for others

Paul begins many letters thanking God for his brothers. Carson shows that this shapes the heart. Those who give thanks for other Christians learn to see God's grace working in them, even with their flaws, and pray with more love and less criticism.

## The prayer and glory of God

In the end, Carson reminds us that the purpose of prayer is not to get God to do our will, but to align our hearts with his. Praying Paul's prayers is learning to desire what God desires: that Christ be known and loved.

This week, read Colossians 1:9-12 and use this prayer for three people in your church, one per day. Change their names in the text and ask God to give them knowledge of His will, fruits, and joy. Then, tell one of them that you prayed.

items.title: Praying like a child
items.author: Paul E. Miller
items.work: A Praying Life (2009)
items.body:
Paul Miller wrote about prayer from ordinary life: a large family, a daughter with a disability, full days, and fatigue. He does not speak as someone who masters the subject, but as someone who has learned, slowly, to depend on God. That is why so many readers recognize themselves in what he writes.

## Come messy

Miller notes that many Christians don't pray because they think they first need to get their mind and heart right. But children don't do that. They come to the Father as they are, talking about everything at once. Jesus teaches us to call God Father. Prayer begins when we stop pretending and go to Him with our mess.

## Helplessness is the way

For the author, feeling weak is not an obstacle to praying; it is the very invitation. Those who think they can do it alone do not pray. Prayer is born when we recognize that we cannot take care of children, marriage, work, or our own heart. Helplessness, given to God, becomes faith.

## The cynicism that cools down

Miller also deals with a silent enemy: cynicism. After prayers that seem unanswered, the heart learns to be suspicious. It calls us to remember that God is writing a bigger story, and that often only afterwards do we see how He responded. Writing down requests and answers helps us perceive God's hand.

## Midday prayer

Finally, Miller shows that praying is not just a separate moment, but an ongoing conversation. Small prayers in traffic, in the kitchen, or before a meeting keep the heart turned toward the Father.

Take a notebook or your cell phone today and write down three concrete requests for your family. Pray for them with simple words, like a child would speak to their father. In a month, return to the list and see what God has done, including what He has changed in you.

links.label: Search: Paul Miller, A Praying Life

items.title: The hole in our holiness
items.author: Kevin DeYoung
items.work: The Hole in Our Holiness (2012)
items.body:
Kevin DeYoung, a Presbyterian pastor in the United States, noticed a curious gap in the church of his time. Many Christians speak enthusiastically about grace, gospel, and social justice, but little about personal holiness. It seems the topic has become outdated or dangerous. For him, this is a hole that needs to be filled.

## Holiness is not optional

DeYoung reminds us that the Bible does not treat holiness as an extra for more dedicated Christians. Without it, Hebrews says, no one will see the Lord. This does not mean we are saved for being holy, but that those who have been saved are called and empowered to grow in holiness. God did not save us to leave us as we were.

## Grace and effort together

One common fear is that talking about effort contradicts grace. DeYoung answers that grace is not opposed to effort, but to merit. Paul commands salvation to be developed with fear and trembling, because it is God who works in us. The Christian fights, prays, reads, flees temptation, and does good, but does all this supported by the work of Christ and the power of the Spirit.

## God delights in us

Another beautiful point of the book is that God can rejoice in the obedience of His children. Our works do not buy the Father's love, but He delights in them as a father delights in the footsteps of the little son. This frees us both from arrogance and from the feeling that nothing we do matters.

## No shortcuts

DeYoung insists that growth is often slow and common. It comes through the Word, through prayer, through fellowship in church, through the Lord's Supper, and through confession. There are no spectacular shortcuts, but there is God's faithfulness.

Choose this week a specific sin you have tolerated. Confess it to God, ask a mature brother for help, and decide on a practical step to escape it. Do this with hope: the same God who called you is the one who will complete the work.

items.title: A greater love drives out the lesser
items.author: Thomas Chalmers
items.work: The Expulsive Power of a New Affection (sermon The Expulsive Power of a New Affection)
items.body:
Thomas Chalmers was a pastor, teacher, and church leader in 19th-century Scotland. Among many sermons, one became famous for its title and its idea: the force that expels love for the world from the heart is a new, stronger love. This simple intuition helps greatly in the fight against sin.

## The heart never goes empty

Chalmers notes that the human heart cannot stand a vacuum. It always loves something. Therefore, just showing that something is bad rarely makes someone give it up. We can know that a habit harms us and remain attached to it, because the heart does not want to be left without anything to love.

## Why banning alone is not enough

Many try to overcome sin only with willpower and rules. Chalmers does not despise God's law, but shows that it alone does not change desires. Tearing away one love without putting another in its place is like trying to empty a bottle at the bottom of the sea: as soon as the water comes out, another comes in. What expels an affection is a greater affection.

## God revealed in Christ

And what is this greater love? Chalmers points to the gospel. When we see God as He revealed Himself in Christ, full of grace and truth, the heart begins to be drawn. The world loses its brightness not because we close our eyes to Him, but because we open our eyes to something more beautiful. John says that whoever loves the world does not have the Father's love; the opposite is also true.

## Sanctification through contemplation

This changes the way we seek holiness. Besides watching and resisting, we need to contemplate Christ in the Scriptures, in prayer, and in worship. His beauty is the best remedy against the charms of sin.

When temptation comes this week, don't just think about not doing it. Think about whom you love most. Read 1 John 2, give thanks for the Father's love, and ask the Spirit to take the place that sin wants to take.

items.title: Married to God, not just to each other
items.author: Christopher Ash
items.work: Married for God (2007)
items.body:
Christopher Ash, pastor and teacher in England, wrote about marriage from an uncommon question. Instead of starting with what marriage can do for me, he asks why God created marriage. The shift in focus seems small, but it transforms everything.

## The marriage has an owner

Ash reminds us that marriage was not invented by us. It was born in the garden, by God's hands, before the fall. Therefore, its meaning does not depend on fads or passing feelings. The one who created marriage is the one who defines what it is for, and the Bible shows that it exists, above all, for the glory of God.

## A partnership in service

In Genesis 2, God gives man a task: to cultivate and guard the garden. The woman is called the helper who corresponds to her. Ash emphasizes that this word does not indicate inferiority; God himself is called the helper of Israel. Husband and wife are partners in the work God entrusted to them: caring for the world, serving others, receiving and raising children when God gives them, and opening the house to the kingdom.

## Love that looks out

When marriage exists only for the satisfaction of both, it closes off and gets tired. When it exists to serve God, love gains direction. The couple stops asking only if they are happy and starts asking how they can, together, be faithful and useful. Curiously, this is how many find deeper joy.

## Fidelity as a foundation

Ash also speaks of exclusivity and the permanence of the alliance. Sexual fidelity and the promise until death are not prisons, but walls of protection so that love grows in safety.

Talk today with your spouse about a question: how can our marriage serve God and others this month? Choose a concrete gesture together, such as hosting someone for a meal or helping a church family.

items.title: What the Puritans knew about the home
items.author: Leland Ryken
items.work: Worldly Saints: The Puritans as They Really Were, 1986)
items.body:
Leland Ryken, a literature professor in the United States, decided to undo a caricature. Many imagine Puritans as cold, sad, and anti-pleasure people. While studying his writings, Ryken found something else: people who took faith and common life seriously, including marriage and family.

## Marriage valued

Ryken shows that the Puritans reacted to a view that placed celibacy above marriage. For them, marriage was a holy and good vocation, created by God. Their preachers spoke of the love between husband and wife with warmth and beauty, calling the spouse companion and friend. Affection was not a detail, but a duty and a joy.

## The house as a small church

A common image among them was that of the family as a small church. The home was a place of prayer, Bible reading, catechism, and singing. The father was responsible for conducting this domestic service, but the whole house participated. It was not formality, but rather about putting God at the center of the routine.

## Order with love

The Puritans spoke of authority and submission at home, but Ryken emphasizes that they always linked this to love and mutual service. The husband's authority existed to care, not to dominate. Children should honor their parents, and parents should treat their children with patience and wisdom.

## A lesson for today

Ryken does not idealize the Puritans; they also had flaws. But his vision challenges a culture that separates faith from life from home. What they remind us is that the most common place, the kitchen, the table, and the living room, can be a place of worship.

Start this week with something simple: a short Bible reading and a prayer after dinner, at least three times. It doesn't have to last long. Let Colossians 3 be the first text, and ask God that the peace of Christ will govern your home.

items.title: Parents who teach faith at home
items.author: Voddie Baucham Jr.
items.work: Family Driven Faith (2007)
items.body:
Voddie Baucham, a reformed Baptist pastor and preacher known in the United States and Africa, wrote a book that upset many Christian parents. His thesis is clear: the main responsibility for the spiritual formation of children does not lie with Sunday school or youth ministry, but with the father and mother.

## A generation that is drifting apart

Baucham begins with a real concern. Many young people raised in the church abandon the faith when they leave home. He doesn't blame only the culture. He asks if the parents haven't outsourced what God entrusted to them. Taking the children to worship is good, but it doesn't replace teaching the faith in daily life.

## Deuteronomy 6 as a plan

The central text of the book is God's command to Israel: to love the Lord with all your heart and speak His words while sitting at home, walking along the road, lying down, and getting up. Baucham shows that faith is transmitted in everyday life. Conversations at the table, in the car, and before bedtime are opportunities for discipleship.

## The example before the lesson

Children learn more from what they see than from what they hear. That is why the author challenges parents to examine their own hearts. A father who loves the Word, however, asks for forgiveness and treats his wife with honor teaches more than many lessons. True faith begins in the heart of the one who teaches.

## Church and family together

Baucham values the local church and advocates that it support parents rather than take their place. Pastors and teachers help, but the home is the first missionary field.

Choose a fixed time this week to open Deuteronomy 6 with your children. Read some verses, ask a simple question about the text, and pray together. If you don't have children, pray for a family in your church and offer help to tired parents.

items.title: Giving grace to children, not just rules
items.author: Elyse Fitzpatrick e Jessica Thompson
items.work: Give Them Grace (2011)
items.body:
Elyse Fitzpatrick, a Bible counselor, wrote this book together with her daughter, Jessica Thompson, who at the time was raising her own children. Mother and daughter looked honestly at how many Christian parents educate: with good rules, good examples, and little gospel. Their proposal is to place grace at the center of raising children.

## Good children are not enough

The authors warn of a subtle danger. We can raise educated, obedient, and morally correct children who never understood they need a Savior. When the main message of home is to be good and God will love you, we teach a religion of merit. The Bible shows another way: we are loved because Christ was good in our place.

## The law and the gospel at home

This does not mean abandoning rules. God's law shows what is right and reveals sin, including that of children. But after correcting, parents should point to Christ, who forgives and transforms. Discipline, then, is not just punishment; it is an occasion to remind the child that they need grace, as both father and mother do.

## Parents who also sin

One of the most liberating points of the book is that parents don't need to pretend to be perfect. When they make mistakes, they can ask their children for forgiveness. This shows, in practice, that everyone in the house lives with the same mercy.

## Rest for tired parents

Finally, the authors remind us that the salvation of children does not depend on the parents' technique. We are called to be faithful, but it is God who changes hearts. This truth takes a huge burden off our shoulders.

The next time you need to correct your child, end the conversation by talking about Jesus: his forgiveness and the love that does not change. Read Ephesians 6:4 and ask God not to provoke your children to anger, but to raise them in the discipline and care of the Lord.

items.title: When fear speaks loudly
items.author: Edward T. Welch
items.work: Running Scared: Fear, Worry, and the God of Rest (2007)
items.body:
Edward Welch, a biblical counselor and psychologist by training, spent years listening to anxious people. Instead of treating fear just as a problem to be eliminated, he sees it as a window to the heart. Fear reveals what we love and what we trust.

## Fear has a message

Welch notes that we care about what is important to us: children, health, money, reputation, the future. Fear is like a voice that says: you will lose something you need. Listening to that voice carefully helps us realize where the heart is supported. Sometimes we find that we place our security in things that cannot sustain it.

## God speaks first

The good news is that God responds to fear with words. One of the most repeated phrases in the Bible is do not fear. Welch shows that this command never comes alone. It comes accompanied by a promise: I am with you, I am your God, I help you. God does not command us to be courageous on our own, but calls us to trust in His presence.

## Daily bread

An important lesson from the book is that of manna. God fed Israel in the desert with enough for one day at a time. Anxiety tries to live tomorrow ahead of time. Jesus teaches us to ask for today's bread and to leave tomorrow in the Father's hands. Grace comes in the measure of the day.

## A kingdom that does not shake

Welch ends by pointing to the kingdom of God. When the heart first seeks the kingdom, other things take their place. We do not stop taking care of responsibilities, but we begin to do so with rest.

When worry tightens today, ask: what am I afraid to lose? Then, read Matthew 6:25-34 and turn worry into a request. If anxiety is intense and constant, also seek help from a pastor and a health professional; this is not a lack of faith.

items.title: Strong castle in times of fear
items.author: Martinho Lutero
items.work: Anthem Strong Castle is Our God (Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott)
items.body:
Few hymns have been sung as much in church history as Castle Forte, written by Martin Luther from Psalm 46. Luther knew fear firsthand: death threats, illness, family losses, and intense spiritual struggles. His hymn was not born from a quiet life, but from a faith that learned to take refuge in God.

## God is our refuge

Psalm 46 begins by saying that God is refuge and strength, a help very present in tribulations. Luther turned this truth into an image: a strong castle, where the persecuted takes shelter. Fear makes us seek shelter in many places. The hymn reminds us that only God is a truly safe place.

## Our strength is not enough

Luther sings honestly that, with our strength, we can do nothing; soon we would be lost. This is liberating. Faith does not require us to be strong. It invites us to admit weakness and look to the one who fights for us. In the hymn, this defender has a name: Jesus Christ, the Lord of hosts.

## The enemy has already been judged

The hymn speaks of the devil as a terrible and cunning enemy. Luther does not minimize evil. But he states that one word alone is enough to overthrow it. Christ's victory on the cross and in the resurrection means that evil will not have the last word. Therefore, we can face fear without being dominated by it.

## The kingdom remains

In the final stanza, Luther says they can take possessions, honor, family, and even life, but the kingdom of God remains. This is not disdain for good things, but the certainty that, in Christ, nothing eternal can be taken from us.

Read Psalm 46 aloud today and, if you can, sing or listen to Strong Castle. Then, repeat verse 10 for a few minutes in silence: be quiet and know that I am God. Give him the fear that weighs most now.

items.title: When God weeps with those who weep
items.author: Joni Eareckson Tada e Steven Estes
items.work: When God Weeps (1997)
items.body:
Joni Eareckson Tada became quadriplegic at seventeen after diving in shallow water. Since then, she has lived in a wheelchair and served people with disabilities around the world. In this book, written with Pastor Steven Estes, she addresses suffering not as a theory, but as someone who carries it every day.

## The question that never disappears

Joni does not hide that he struggled with God. There were phases of revolt, depression, and unanswered questions. The book does not offer ready-made phrases. It begins by acknowledging that pain is real and that the Bible does not ask us to pretend everything is okay. The lamenting psalms show that we can lead God to our complaint.

## A sovereign and good God

The authors state, with reformed faith, that nothing escapes God's government, not even suffering. This may seem harsh at first glance. But they show that the alternative would be much worse: a world where pain happens senselessly and without control. Because God reigns, suffering has limits and purpose, even when we don't understand it.

## God also suffered

The center of the book is the cross. God does not watch pain from afar. In Christ, He entered into suffering, was wounded, abandoned, and killed. The God who governs is the same who weeps. That is why we can trust that He understands us and that He turns even the worst wounds into instruments of grace.

## A glory that comes

Joni speaks joyfully of the hope of the resurrection. She looks forward to the day when she will dance with new legs. The present afflictions, Paul says, produce an eternal weight of glory. This does not lessen the pain, but places it within a larger story.

If you are suffering, read 2 Corinthians 4:16-18 slowly and tell God, sincerely, what hurts. If you know someone who is suffering, visit that person this week. Speak little, listen a lot, and pray with them.

items.title: Letters written in distress
items.author: Samuel Rutherford
items.work: Letters of Samuel Rutherford (17th century)
items.body:
Samuel Rutherford was a 17th-century Scottish pastor, minister in a small rural parish, and later a theology professor. Because of his convictions, he was removed from the pulpit and sent away from his congregation. From that time of exile came many letters to friends, church members, and bereaved families. They are still read today as a treasure of consolation.

## Sweeter Christ in the test

The theme running through the letters is the love of Christ. Rutherford said he had never known so much of the Savior's sweetness as he did in times of suffering. This does not mean he liked to suffer, but that he found in the trial a deeper communion with the Lord. The cross that weighed became for him a place of encounter.

## Words to those who weep

Many letters were written to parents who lost children and to widows. Rutherford did not despise tears. He cried with those who wept. But he also remembered that those who die in the Lord are not lost; they went only ahead, to the Father's house. The separation is real, but temporary.

## The God who works in pain

Rutherford saw God's hand even in afflictions. He compared the Lord to a gardener who prunes plants so they bear more fruit. Pruning hurts, but it is not cruelty. It is the care of those who know what they are doing.

## The eyes on eternity

Another mark of the letters is the longing for heaven. Rutherford wrote as someone who already smelled the scent of glory. That hope gave strength to remain faithful, even far from home and the pulpit.

Think of someone who is going through grief or a long trial. Write that person a short message, by hand or on their phone, with a verse from Isaiah 43 and the promise that you are praying. Sometimes, a simple letter is how God comforts.

items.title: Signs of a healthy church
items.author: Mark Dever
items.work: Nine Marks of a Healthy Church (Nine Marks of a Healthy Church, 2000)
items.body:
Mark Dever, a Baptist pastor in Washington, United States, was concerned with a question that seems simple: what makes a church healthy? At a time when success was measured by numbers, events, and programs, he turned to the Scriptures and proposed some marks that help evaluate the life of a congregation.

## The Word at the Center

The first mark, and the most important, is expository preaching: the one in which the sermon shows what the biblical text says and applies it to life. For Deer, the church is born and grows by the Word of God. When the pulpit faithfully explains the Bible, the flock is fed and God speaks to His people.

## Gospel and conversion well understood

Duty insists that the church needs clarity about the gospel: God is holy, we are sinners, Christ died and rose again, and we are called to repentance and faith. Without this clarity, the church risks confusing conversion with an emotional decision or a change in behavior.

## Membership and mutual care

Another mark is membership taken seriously. Being a member is not having your name on a list, but making a commitment of love to concrete brothers. Duty also speaks of discipline in the church, which, when done with humility and patience, is an act of care that protects and restores.

## Leadership and discipleship

Finally, he values biblical leadership, with qualified elders, and a culture of discipleship, in which more mature Christians help the younger ones grow. The health of the church does not depend on a famous leader, but on a people who build themselves up.

Read Acts 2:42-47 this week and ask: what of this description already exists in my church and where can I help? Choose a person from the congregation to talk to, pray, and read the Bible together this month.

items.title: Communion is a gift
items.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (com uma leitura reformada)
items.work: Life in Communion (Gemeinsames Leben, 1939)
items.body:
Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a German Lutheran pastor who opposed Nazism and was executed in the final days of World War II. Before that, he ran an underground seminary where future pastors lived together. From this experience was born a short book about communal life among Christians, which remains relevant for the church today.

## Communion is grace

Bonhoeffer begins by reminding us that being able to be with other Christians is a privilege, not something guaranteed. Many brothers live imprisoned, isolated, or persecuted. Therefore, every service, every meal with the church, and every visit from a brother must be received with gratitude, as a gift from God.

## The dream that needs to die

One of the strongest ideas in the book is that God destroys our idealized dreams of community. We arrive at church expecting perfect people and soon become disappointed. Bonhoeffer says this disappointment is healthy. Christian communion is not an ideal we built, but a reality God created in Christ. We love real brothers, with their flaws, because Christ loved them.

## The ministry of listening

Bonhoeffer speaks of simple services that keep communion alive: holding your tongue, being humble, helping with small things, carrying others' burdens, and above all, listening. Many Christians always want to speak, teach, and correct. Listening attentively is a form of love.

## Confession and forgiveness

The book ends with the confession of sins among brothers. Bonhoeffer sees in it a way to break the isolation of sin. A reformed reading reminds us that confession is neither a sacrament nor a condition for forgiveness, but recognizes that confessing and praying for one another, as James commands, brings healing and humility.

Thank God today for three brothers in your church, naming them. Then, look for one of them this week just to listen: ask how he is and don't rush to talk.

items.title: Baptism and Supper in the Baptist Confession of 1689
items.author: Tradição batista reformada
items.work: Baptist Confession of Faith of 1689, chapters 28 to 30
items.body:
The Baptist Confession of Faith of 1689 was written by Baptist churches in England that wanted to show their unity with other Reformers. It closely follows the Westminster Confession in almost everything, but differs on one important point: who should be baptized. Knowing this view helps to understand Baptist brothers and to converse with respect.

## Ordinances of Christ

Confession calls baptism and the Supper ordinances instituted by the Lord Jesus Himself. They were not invented by the church and should not be altered by it. They must be administered in the local church, by those who have been called to do so, until the end of the world.

## The baptism of those who believe

In the chapter on baptism, Confession teaches that it is a sign of the believer's union with Christ in his death and resurrection, of grafting into him, of forgiveness of sins, and of surrendering oneself to God to live in newness of life. Therefore, it states that the proper subjects of baptism are those who profess repentance and faith. And it understands that immersion is the appropriate form. Presbyterian and Reformed continental brothers also baptize the children of believers, based on the covenant. It is a real difference, seriously debated, between people who confess the same gospel.

## The Supper as spiritual food

Regarding the Supper, the 1689 Confession is very close to Westminster. It rejects the idea that bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, and also denies that the Supper is merely an empty memory. Those who participate in faith receive and feed on the crucified Christ, in a real but spiritual way. The Supper also expresses the communion of believers among themselves.

## Grace, not merit

None of the ordinances save by itself. They point to Christ and strengthen the faith of those who receive Him.

If you were baptized, remember today what your baptism says: you died and rose with Christ. Read Romans 6 and prepare your heart for the next Supper, with confession and gratitude.
