items.title: The Supper that nourishes faith
items.author: Keith Mathison
items.work: Given for You: Reclaiming Calvin's Doctrine of the Lord's Supper (2002)
items.body:
Keith Mathison, a theology professor linked to the Ligonier ministry, wrote a book to remind Reformed churches of a treasure many had forgotten: John Calvin's view of the Last Supper. He realized that many evangelicals treat the Supper merely as a moment of remembrance, and that this impoverishes church life.

## More than memory

Mathison shows that Calvin rejected two extremes. On one side, the idea that bread and wine physically become the body and blood of Christ. On the other, the idea that the Supper is just a symbol to recall something distant. For Calvin, and for Reformed confessions, at the Supper Christ truly nourishes us, not physically, but by the power of the Holy Spirit.

## The Spirit unites heaven and earth

How is this possible if Christ ascended to heaven? Mathison explains Calvin's answer: the Holy Spirit is the bond that unites us to Christ. We do not pull Christ down; the Spirit lifts our hearts to Him. That is why the ancient liturgy told the people: lift up your hearts. At the Supper, faith receives the living Christ.

## A means of grace

The author reminds us that the Supper is not a reward for perfect Christians, but food for the weak. It strengthens faith, confirms promises, and deepens communion with Christ and the church. Those who examine themselves do not seek to discover if they are worthy on their own, but are trusting in Christ and reconciling with their brothers and sisters.

## A table for the church

Mathison also challenges churches to value the Supper in worship, celebrating it with reverence and joy. Calvin, he recalls, desired frequent celebration.

Before the next Supper at your church, read 1 Corinthians 11:23-29. Confess your sins, try to resolve some grief with a brother, and go to the table expecting to be nourished by Christ, not because of your strength, but because of His grace.

items.title: Expecting great things from God
items.author: William Carey
items.work: An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792)
items.body:
William Carey was an English shoemaker, poor and with almost no formal education, but passionate about the Bible and the world. While repairing shoes, he studied languages and maps. In 1792 he published a small book that helped ignite the modern missionary movement. The following year, he left for India, where he served until the end of his life.

## The Great Commission is still valid

Many Christians at the time thought that Jesus' command to make disciples of all nations had been only for the apostles. Carey answered with a simple question: if Jesus' promise to be with us until the end of time still holds, why wouldn't the command hold? The mission belongs to the church of all generations.

## Using the means

The book's title speaks of using means. Carey firmly believes in God's sovereignty in salvation, but understood that God uses instruments. Just as merchants cross seas for profit, Christians should organize, pray, offer, and send people out of love for Christ. He proposed the creation of a missionary society, and the Baptists in his region founded it.

## Wait and start

In a sermon that same year, Carey summed up his vision in a famous phrase: expect great things from God; try great things for God. Order matters. First we trust in the Lord's promises, then we act with courage.

## Perseverance in the field

In India, Carey faced years without conversions, illnesses, and painful family losses. Even so, he persevered. He worked with colleagues translating the Scriptures into several languages and left a planted church.

Read Matthew 28:18-20 and ask how you can use the means God has given you. Choose a missionary or an unreached people to pray this week and, if possible, set aside an offering for your church's missionary work.

items.title: The gospel that arrived in Brazil
items.author: Ashbel Green Simonton
items.work: Diary and ministry in Brazil (from 1859 onward)
items.body:
Ashbel Green Simonton was a young Presbyterian pastor from the United States when he felt the call to serve in Brazil. He arrived in Rio de Janeiro in 1859, just over twenty-five years old. He died a few years later, still young, but planted the seed of the Presbyterian Church in the country. His story teaches a lot about mission.

## Learn before you speak

Simonton dedicated his first months to learning Portuguese and getting to know Brazilian culture. He knew the gospel needed to be communicated in the language of the people. It began with small meetings, Bible classes, and personal conversations. The mission did not begin with grand events, but with patience and humility.

## The Word as seed

The center of Simonton's work was the Bible. He preached, taught, and distributed the Scriptures, trusting that the Word of God would do its work. He also helped found an evangelical newspaper, the Evangelical Press, to take the message further. He believed that faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the Word of Christ.

## Church and leadership training

In a short time, the first Brazilians were baptized and a church was organized in Rio de Janeiro. Simonton understood that the mission does not end with conversion. It was necessary to form the church and prepare Brazilian pastors. He dedicated himself to teaching young people who would later continue the work.

## Fidelity amid pain

Simonton faced harsh personal losses, including the death of his wife a few years after arriving. Still, he remained faithful until the end. His short life shows that God measures faithfulness, not just length of service.

Read Romans 10:13-17 today and thank God for those who brought the gospel to Brazil. Then, think of someone close to you who does not yet know Christ and ask God for an opportunity to talk with them this week.

items.title: A Bible breathed by God
items.author: B. B. Warfield
items.work: The Inspiration and Authority of the Bible (The Inspiration and Authority of the Bible, 1948 collection)
items.body:
Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield was a professor at Princeton Seminary for more than thirty years, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. At a time when many scholars were beginning to treat the Bible as a merely human book, Warfield wrote with rigor and piety about the inspiration of the Scriptures. His essays on the subject were later collected in a volume that is still a reference.

## What Paul meant

Warfield carefully studied the word Paul uses in 2 Timothy 3:16, translated as inspired. He showed that meaning is breathed by God. The idea is not that God breathed something special on a human text, but that Scripture came from the mouth of God. That is why it has the authority of God Himself.

## God and human authors

At the same time, Warfield did not ignore human authors. Moses, David, Luke, and Paul wrote with their styles, vocabularies, and experiences. For him, God prepared these men throughout their lives and led them in such a way that they wrote exactly what He wanted. The Bible is entirely the word of God and the entire human word, without one thing nullifying the other.

## The testimony of Jesus

Warfield liked to remind us that trust in the Bible is not a church invention. It is the stance of Jesus himself and the apostles, who cited the Old Testament as the word of God and said that Scripture cannot fail. Following Christ includes receiving the Bible as he received it.

## What is it used for

Paul says that Scripture is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and educating in righteousness. Warfield never separated doctrine from life. An inspired Bible is a Bible that must be read, believed, and obeyed.

Read 2 Timothy 3 today. Before opening the Bible in the coming days, say a short prayer: Lord, speak, for your servant hears. Read expecting to hear the voice of God, not just information.

items.title: How do we know that the Bible belongs to God?
items.author: João Calvino
items.work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, chapters 6 to 9 (1559)
items.body:
One of the oldest questions about the Bible is this: how can we be sure that it is the Word of God? In the time of John Calvin, some said that the church is the one who gives authority to the Scriptures. In the early parts of the Institutes, Calvin answers differently and in a deeply comforting way.

## The glasses of Scripture

Calvin compares the Bible to glasses. A person with weak eyesight sees a book as a blur; with glasses, they can read. Likewise, creation shows the glory of God, but our vision was blurred by sin. Scripture helps us see clearly who God is and who we are. That is why we need it.

## The church does not give authority to the Bible

For Calvin, saying that the Bible depends on the church's approval is to turn things around. The church was built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets. Scripture comes first, and the church recognizes it, as a sheep recognizes the voice of the shepherd.

## The Inner Testimony of the Spirit

The deepest certainty, Calvin says, comes from the Holy Spirit. The same Spirit who spoke through the prophets speaks to our hearts and convinces us that they faithfully transmitted what God said. Arguments about the beauty, coherence, and history of the Bible help and confirm, but they are not the foundation. Faith rests on the voice of God, which is heard through the Word itself.

## Word and Spirit together

Calvin also warned against those who claimed to have revelations of the Spirit apart from the Bible. The Spirit does not bring a new message; it seals and illuminates Scripture. Separating the two is losing both.

Read Psalm 19 today and notice how David moves from the glory of heaven to the perfection of the Lord's law. Then, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes to see the wonders of the Word and to give you joy in obeying it.

items.title: The Trinity at the heart of the gospel
items.author: Fred Sanders
items.work: The Deep Things of God: How the Trinity Changes Everything (2010)
items.body:
Fred Sanders, a theology professor in the United States, wrote for ordinary Christians who find the doctrine of the Trinity important but distant. His thesis surprises: evangelicals already live the Trinity, often without realizing it. The gospel we believe, the prayer we say, and the salvation we receive have a Trinitarian form.

## The gospel is Trinitarian

Sanders shows that you cannot tell the good news without talking about the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. The Father sends the Son, the Son becomes man, dies and rises, and the Spirit is poured out to unite us to Christ. Salvation is not the work of a solitary God, but of the God who is an eternal communion of love.

## First of all, love

A beautiful point of the book is to remember that God did not need us to be happy. Before creation, the Father loved the Son in the Spirit. God did not create the world out of want, but out of generosity. When He saves us, He invites us to participate in a love that already existed.

## Prayer with address

Sanders notes that Christian prayer has a direction: we pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Paul says that, through Christ, we have access to the Father in one Spirit. This does not mean that we cannot speak with the Son or with the Spirit, but that prayer places us within the life of the triune God.

## A doctrine for life

The Trinity, says Sanders, is not a puzzle for experts. It is the revelation of who God is. Knowing the Father, the Son, and the Spirit better deepens our worship and our security.

Read Ephesians 1:3-14 and mark what each person of the Trinity does for their salvation. Then, pray giving thanks to the Father you chose, the Son who redeemed, and the Spirit who sealed you.

items.title: Glory to the Father, the Son, and the Spirit
items.author: Basílio de Cesareia
items.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto, c. 375)
items.body:
Basil was bishop of Caesarea, in Cappadocia, in the 4th century. He lived at a time when the church was still struggling to clearly express faith in the Trinity. After the Council of Nicaea, many accepted the divinity of the Son, but some denied that the Holy Spirit was fully God. Basil wrote a treatise to defend the biblical faith.

## A discussion about praise

The debate began with a liturgical phrase. Basil sometimes gave glory to the Father with the Son, along with the Holy Spirit. Some critics said that one could only say to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, as if the Spirit were on a lower level. Basil showed that both forms are biblical, but that worship of the Spirit together with the Father and the Son is legitimate because He is God.

## The Spirit in God's work

Basil argued based on the Scriptures. The Spirit participates in creation, inspires the prophets, unites believers to Christ, sanctifies, and gives life. No one but God can do these things. Furthermore, Jesus orders baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, placing the three side by side.

## Faith and worship go hand in hand

An important lesson from Basil is that what we believe is shown in the way we worship. The church baptized and praised in the name of the Trinity before having detailed theological formulas. He understood that doctrine serves to protect and clarify the praise of God's people.

## A common inheritance

Basil's work helped prepare the confession of the Council of Constantinople in 381, which affirmed that the Holy Spirit is Lord and giver of life and is worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son.

Read Matthew 28 today and pay attention to the words of baptism. At the next service, when you sing or listen to the Trinitarian blessing, remember that you are worshiping the one God in three persons, as the church has done for centuries.

items.title: True God and true man
items.author: Donald Macleod
items.work: The Person of Christ (1998)
items.body:
Donald Macleod, a professor of theology in Scotland, wrote a careful study on who Jesus Christ is. His book goes through the Bible and church history, but always with a pastoral goal: to help the Christian know and worship the Savior he confesses.

## The Eternal Son

Macleod begins with eternity. Before being born in Bethlehem, the Son already existed, with the Father, as God. John says that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The incarnation was not the beginning of the Son, but the moment when the one who has always existed took on our nature.

## A real humanity

At the same time, Macleod insists that Jesus was fully human. He was hungry, thirsty, and weary. He grew in wisdom, wept before a friend's grave, felt anguish in Gethsemane. He was not God disguised as a man. His humanity is real, and that is why He can represent us and sympathize with our weaknesses.

## One person

The ancient church in Chalcedon confessed that Christ is one person in two natures, without confusion and without separation. Macleod shows that this formula does not complicate faith but protects it. If Christ were not God, He could not save us. If He were not man, He could not die in our place. If He were two persons, the cross would be the work of one man alone.

## Christ who humbled Himself

The author also reflects on the humiliation of the Son, who did not cease to be God, but gave up the glory that belonged to him to serve. In Philippians 2, Paul uses this truth to teach humility to the church. The doctrine of Christ always leads to the imitation of Christ.

Read John 1:1-18 this week and write down everything the text says about the divinity and humanity of Jesus. Then, worship: the same one who created the world became flesh to dwell among us and save you.

items.title: The God who put Himself in our place
items.author: John Stott
items.work: The Cross of Christ (1986)
items.body:
John Stott was an Anglican pastor in London and one of the most influential evangelical leaders of the 20th century. Among his many books, one is considered by many to be his main work: a study on the cross. For Stott, one cannot understand who Jesus is without understanding why he died.

## The cross in the center

Stott begins by recalling that the symbol chosen by Christians was not the manger, nor the empty tomb, but the cross. The Gospels devote a huge part to Jesus' last week. The apostles preached Christ crucified. Jesus' death was not an accident at the end of his life, but the purpose for which he came.

## The problem of forgiveness

Why doesn't God simply forgive? Stott answers that forgiveness is not simple for a holy God. Sin is real, guilt is real, and God's justice cannot be ignored. At the same time, God is love and desires to save. On the cross, God's holiness and love meet.

## The replacement of God by Himself

The central idea of the book is that, on the cross, God put Himself in our place. It was not a third innocent punished by an angry God, but God Himself, in the person of the Son, assuming the penalty that was ours. Isaiah prophesied that the Servant would be wounded by our transgressions. The person of Christ, God and man, is what makes this exchange possible and just.

## Living under the cross

Stott also shows that the cross shapes the Christian life. It humbles us because it shows the magnitude of our sin; it gives us security because it shows the magnitude of God's love; and it teaches us to love our enemies and serve others with sacrifice.

Read Isaiah 53 slowly this week and replace the pronouns we and ours with your name. Then, thank Christ for taking your place and ask for grace to live so that the cross is seen in your life.

items.title: The Spirit who forms Christ in us
items.author: John Owen
items.work: Pneumatology (A Discourse Concerning the Holy Spirit, 1674)
items.body:
John Owen was one of England's greatest Puritan theologians. In a time of much confusion about the Holy Spirit, when some despised Him and others claimed to receive revelations apart from the Bible, Owen wrote a long study on the person and work of the Spirit. His goal was to help believers honor the Spirit as God and recognize His real work.

## The Spirit is a divine person

Owen begins by stating that the Spirit is not a force or energy, but a person of the Trinity, equal to the Father and the Son. He thinks, wills, loves, and can be saddened. Therefore, we must treat Him with reverence and trust, not as a power we use, but as the Lord who guides us.

## The Spirit and Jesus

One of the most beautiful parts of the work shows the Spirit acting in the life of Christ Himself. It was by the Spirit that the Son was conceived in Mary's womb. The Spirit filled him with wisdom, anointed him at baptism, sustained him in temptations, and was present in His offering on the cross. Jesus lived as a true man dependent on the Spirit, and this shows us what the Spirit wants to do in us.

## From death to life

Owen describes regeneration as a work that only the Spirit can accomplish. The sinner is dead and cannot give life to himself. The Spirit enlightens the mind, changes the will, and awakens new affections. Jesus said it is necessary to be born from above, and that the wind blows where it wants.

## Holiness as a fruit

Then, the Spirit continues the work, producing holiness throughout life. Owen does not see sanctification as an isolated effort, but as the believer's cooperation with the grace the Spirit pours out.

Read John 16:7-15 today and pay attention to what Jesus says about the Spirit: he convinces, guides, and glorifies Christ. Pray asking the Spirit to help you see more of Jesus this week and to obey with joy.

items.title: The Spirit that points to Christ
items.author: Augustus Nicodemus Lopes
items.work: Sermons and writings about the person and work of the Holy Spirit
items.body:
Augustus Nicodemus Lopes, a Presbyterian pastor and Brazilian teacher, has dedicated many sermons and texts to the Holy Spirit. In an environment where the topic is often associated with spectacular experiences, he seeks to return to the basic question: what does the Bible say the Spirit does?

## The Spirit glorifies Christ

One point Augustus often highlights is that the Spirit does not draw attention to itself. Jesus said that the Spirit would glorify Him. Therefore, where the Spirit acts, Christ is exalted, the gospel is proclaimed, and people turn to the Savior. A spirituality that revolves around sensations and special people needs to be examined in light of this criterion.

## Word and Spirit

Augustus argues, with the Reformed tradition, that the Spirit acts through Scripture. He was the one who inspired the Bible, and it is he who illuminates it for us. He also holds the cessationist position: the gifts linked to revelation and apostolic signs fulfilled their role in the foundation of the church. There are Reformed brothers who think differently on this point, but all agree that no experience can be above the Word.

## The fruit above the spectacle

For Augustus, the clearest mark of the presence of the Spirit is the fruit described in Galatians 5: love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, faithfulness, meekness, and self-control. This fruit grows slowly, in ordinary life, and is often less visible than an extraordinary event. But it is this fruit that shows the likeness to Christ.

## Gifts to serve

The gifts that the Spirit distributes today, such as teaching, service, mercy, and leadership, exist to build up the church, not to promote those who possess them.

Read Galatians 5:16-26 this week. Choose a virtue from the fruit of the Spirit in which you need to grow and ask God every day to develop it in you. Notice how it may appear in your reactions at home and at work.

items.title: Yes, but not yet
items.author: Anthony Hoekema
items.work: The Bible and the Future (The Bible and the Future, 1979)
items.body:
Anthony Hoekema was a professor of theology in Michigan, United States, and wrote one of the most balanced Reformed studies on the last things. In a time of much speculation about dates and signs, he sought to show what the Bible really teaches about the future and how it affects the present.

## The end has already begun

Hoekema's central idea is that the final era has already begun with the coming of Christ. Jesus announced that the kingdom of God had arrived. In his death and resurrection, the future invaded history. That is why the New Testament calls the present time the last days. We live between the first and second coming, in a time of already and not yet.

## The believer's hope

Hoekema shows that this vision brings balance. We already have the Spirit, forgiveness, and new life, but we do not yet see complete victory. We are already children, but we still groan waiting for the redemption of the body. This protects us both from discouragement and from the illusion that the church will build paradise on its own.

## New earth, not just sky

One of the best-known chapters of the book deals with the new earth. Hoekema reminds us that Christian hope is not to float eternally in the clouds. God will renew all creation. There will be new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells. What God created good and sin spoiled will be restored and glorified.

## Hope that works

Therefore, what we do now has value. Hoekema teaches that hope in Christ's return does not lead to fleeing the world, but to faithful service, holiness, and mission.

Read Revelation 21:1-5 today and imagine, with the help of the text, the house God is preparing. Then, make a list of two things you can do this week as a sign of that hope: an act of justice, mercy, or reconciliation.

items.title: The rest that awaits us
items.author: Richard Baxter
items.work: The Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650)
items.body:
Richard Baxter foi um pastor puritano inglês, conhecido pelo cuidado com o seu rebanho em Kidderminster. Ainda jovem, adoeceu gravemente e pensou que ia morrer. Nesse tempo, começou a meditar no céu, e dessas meditações nasceu um dos livros devocionais mais lidos do puritanismo.

## O descanso prometido

Baxter partiu de Hebreus 4: resta um descanso para o povo de Deus. Para ele, esse descanso não é ociosidade, mas o fim de todo cansaço do pecado, da dor e da luta. É a alegria de estar com Deus, vê-lo e amá-lo sem nenhum obstáculo. Tudo o que a vida cristã busca encontra ali a sua plenitude.

## Pensar no céu faz bem

Baxter insistia que os cristãos deviam meditar com frequência na glória futura. Ele acreditava que muitos crentes vivem tristes e mornos porque quase nunca pensam no que os espera. Assim como um viajante cansado ganha forças ao lembrar da casa, o cristão se fortalece ao lembrar do seu destino. A meditação no céu não tira o pé do chão; dá firmeza para caminhar.

## Consolo para as aflições

O próprio Baxter viveu com dores e enfermidades durante grande parte da vida. Ele não negava o sofrimento, mas o colocava em perspectiva. As lutas de agora são curtas comparadas ao descanso eterno. Essa esperança ajuda o crente a suportar as perdas sem desespero.

## Motivação para servir

Ao mesmo tempo, Baxter era um pastor muito ativo. A esperança do céu o impulsionava a visitar famílias, catequizar e pregar. Quem sabe para onde vai deseja levar outros consigo.

Separe dez minutos nesta semana para ler Hebreus 4 e meditar no descanso que Deus prometeu. Pense no que mais lhe cansa hoje e diga a Deus: isso não é para sempre. Depois, agradeça por Cristo, que garante esse descanso a quem confia nele.

items.title: Por que Deus se importa com quem dorme com quem?
items.author: Sam Allberry
items.work: Why Does God Care Who I Sleep With? (2020)
items.body:
Sam Allberry, pastor e escritor britânico, escreveu um livro curto para pessoas que acham a ética sexual cristã estranha ou ultrapassada. Ele não começa com proibições, mas com uma pergunta honesta: por que Deus se importaria com algo tão pessoal? A resposta, segundo ele, revela muito sobre quem Deus é e sobre quem nós somos.

## O corpo importa

Allberry lembra que, para a Bíblia, o corpo não é um detalhe. Deus o criou, Cristo o assumiu na encarnação e o ressuscitará. Paulo diz que o corpo é para o Senhor e que somos templo do Espírito. Por isso, aquilo que fazemos com o corpo não é indiferente. O sexo envolve a pessoa inteira, não apenas um momento de prazer.

## O sexo foi feito para a aliança

O autor mostra que Deus não é contra o sexo; foi ele quem o criou. Mas o criou para o casamento entre um homem e uma mulher, uma aliança de compromisso para a vida toda. Fora desse lugar, o sexo promete intimidade, mas costuma deixar feridas, comparação e vazio. Dentro da aliança, ele expressa uma entrega que não é retirada no dia seguinte.

## Uma história maior

Allberry também aponta que o casamento é uma imagem do amor de Cristo pela igreja. Por isso a fidelidade sexual é tão importante: ela conta, na vida comum, a história de um Deus que não abandona o seu povo. Solteiros que vivem em castidade também testemunham essa história, mostrando que Cristo é suficiente.

## Graça para quem já errou

O livro não fala de cima para baixo. Allberry lembra que todos falhamos e que o evangelho oferece perdão completo. Paulo, depois de listar pecados sexuais, diz aos coríntios: tais fostes alguns de vós, mas fostes lavados.

Leia 1 Coríntios 6:9-20 com calma. Se você luta nessa área, procure um pastor ou um irmão de confiança e converse com honestidade. Lembre-se: em Cristo há perdão e força para recomeçar, e a igreja deve acolher você nesse caminho.

links.label: Busca: Sam Allberry, Why Does God Care Who I Sleep With?

items.title: Dá-me castidade, mas não agora
items.author: Agostinho de Hipona
items.work: Confissões, livro VIII (c. 400)
items.body:
Antes de se tornar um dos maiores teólogos da igreja, Agostinho viveu anos preso a desejos que não conseguia vencer. Nas Confissões, ele conta com uma honestidade rara a sua luta com a sexualidade e o caminho até a conversão. Sua história ajuda muitos jovens cristãos que se sentem divididos entre o que creem e o que desejam.

## Uma vontade dividida

Agostinho descreve como, já convencido da verdade do cristianismo, ainda não queria deixar os prazeres. Ele confessa ter orado, ainda jovem: dá-me castidade e continência, mas não agora. A frase é sincera e incômoda. Muitos querem a pureza, mas não hoje. Agostinho mostra que essa divisão interior é escravidão, e que adiar a obediência é uma forma de dizer não a Deus.

## O peso do hábito

Ele explica que o costume vira corrente. Cada vez que cedemos ao desejo desordenado, a corrente fica mais forte, até que sentimos que não conseguimos mais sair. Agostinho não minimiza essa realidade. Ele sabia que, sozinho, não teria forças.

## Tome e leia

No famoso episódio do jardim, em Milão, Agostinho chorava sob uma figueira quando ouviu uma voz de criança que repetia: tome e leia. Abriu as cartas de Paulo e leu Romanos 13: não em orgias e bebedeiras, não em impudicícias e dissoluções, mas revesti-vos do Senhor Jesus Cristo e nada disponhais para a carne. Naquele momento, diz ele, uma luz de segurança encheu o seu coração.

## A graça que liberta

A lição de Agostinho é que a castidade não nasce apenas de força de vontade, mas da graça de Deus que nos dá um novo amor. Cristo não apenas proíbe; ele liberta e satisfaz.

Se você tem adiado a obediência nessa área, leia Romanos 13:11-14 hoje. Dê um passo concreto: corte uma fonte de tentação, como um aplicativo, um site ou um relacionamento, e procure alguém maduro na igreja para orar com você. Deus perdoa e restaura quem se volta para ele.

items.title: Uma pergunta decide o debate
items.author: Scott Klusendorf
items.work: The Case for Life (2009)
items.body:
Scott Klusendorf é um defensor da vida que passou anos ensinando cristãos a falar sobre o aborto com clareza e respeito. Ele percebeu que muitos crentes são contra o aborto, mas não sabem explicar por quê. Em seu livro, propõe que o debate inteiro gira em torno de uma única pergunta: o que é o nascituro?

## A pergunta central

Klusendorf argumenta que, se o nascituro não é um ser humano, nenhuma justificativa para o aborto é necessária. Mas, se é um ser humano, nenhuma justificativa é suficiente. Questões como privacidade, escolha e dificuldades econômicas são importantes, mas não autorizam tirar a vida de um inocente. Afinal, não aceitaríamos essas razões para matar uma criança de dois anos.

## O que a ciência mostra

O autor lembra que a embriologia ensina que a vida de um novo ser humano começa na concepção. Desde o início, ele é um organismo distinto, vivo e humano, que se desenvolve. A Bíblia confirma isso quando Davi diz que Deus o formou no ventre da mãe e o conhecia antes que nascesse.

## Diferenças que não mudam o valor

Klusendorf mostra que as diferenças entre um embrião e um adulto são de tamanho, nível de desenvolvimento, ambiente e grau de dependência. Nenhuma delas muda o valor de uma pessoa. Um bebê é menor e mais dependente que um adolescente, mas não vale menos. A dignidade humana vem de sermos imagem de Deus.

## Verdade com graça

O autor insiste que a defesa da vida deve ser feita com amor. Muitas mulheres que abortaram carregam culpa e dor. A igreja deve anunciar o perdão de Cristo e acolher, além de apoiar gestantes em situação difícil, com cuidado prático.

Leia o Salmo 139 nesta semana. Se você já passou por um aborto, saiba que em Cristo há perdão completo; procure um pastor para conversar. E pergunte à sua igreja como apoiar mães em situação de vulnerabilidade.

links.label: Psalm 139 in the Bible of SOLA

items.title: Respostas que protegem a vida
items.author: Randy Alcorn
items.work: ProLife Answers to ProChoice Arguments (1992)
items.body:
Randy Alcorn, pastor e escritor nos Estados Unidos, reuniu num livro respostas claras para os argumentos mais comuns a favor do aborto. Seu objetivo não era ganhar discussões, mas ajudar cristãos a pensar, falar com mansidão e agir em favor das crianças e de suas mães.

## Ouvir os argumentos

Alcorn começa levando a sério o que as pessoas dizem. Argumentos como meu corpo, minhas regras, ninguém pode impor a sua religião ou é melhor abortar do que nascer numa família pobre merecem resposta cuidadosa. Ele mostra que muitos deles pressupõem que o nascituro não é uma pessoa. Quando essa premissa é examinada, a força do argumento muda.

## Dois corpos, não um

Sobre a ideia de que o feto é parte do corpo da mãe, Alcorn lembra que o bebê tem o próprio código genético, o próprio coração e, muitas vezes, um sexo diferente do da mãe. Ele está no corpo dela, mas não é o corpo dela. Isso não diminui a mulher; mostra que há duas vidas que merecem cuidado.

## Deus conhece antes do nascimento

O autor recorre às Escrituras para mostrar o valor da vida no ventre. Deus diz a Jeremias: antes que eu te formasse no ventre, eu te conheci. João Batista se alegrou no ventre de Isabel. A Bíblia trata a criança antes do nascimento como alguém, e não como algo.

## Compaixão em ação

Alcorn insiste que ser pró-vida significa também apoiar mulheres grávidas em dificuldade, cuidar de crianças, incentivar a adoção e oferecer esperança a quem já abortou. A cruz de Cristo é suficiente para perdoar todo pecado, inclusive esse.

Leia Jeremias 1:4-10 hoje e agradeça a Deus pelo valor que ele dá a cada vida. Se você carrega a dor de um aborto, saiba que pode levá-la a Cristo e encontrar perdão e paz; converse com um pastor. Pense também em uma forma concreta de apoiar uma gestante ou uma família que precisa.

items.title: Fazer as pazes em casa
items.author: Ken Sande
items.work: O Pacificador (The Peacemaker, 1991)
items.body:
Ken Sande, advogado e conselheiro cristão, fundou um ministério dedicado a ajudar pessoas a resolver conflitos à luz do evangelho. Seu livro trata de brigas na igreja, no trabalho e entre vizinhos, mas é especialmente útil no casamento, onde os conflitos são frequentes e as feridas ficam perto.

## O conflito como oportunidade

Sande propõe uma mudança de olhar: o conflito não é só um problema, é uma oportunidade de glorificar a Deus, servir o outro e crescer em semelhança a Cristo. Em vez de perguntar como ganhar a briga, o casal pode perguntar como Deus será honrado nessa situação.

## Primeiro a trave no meu olho

Um dos princípios mais conhecidos do livro vem das palavras de Jesus: tire primeiro a trave do seu olho. Antes de apontar o erro do cônjuge, cada um deve examinar a própria parte. Sande ensina que uma confissão verdadeira é específica, assume a responsabilidade sem desculpas, reconhece a dor causada e pede perdão. Dizer desculpe se você se ofendeu não é confessar.

## Corrigir com mansidão

Há momentos em que é preciso falar sobre o pecado do outro. Sande lembra que isso deve ser feito com mansidão, no momento certo e com o objetivo de restaurar, não de humilhar. O tom e a intenção importam tanto quanto as palavras.

## Perdoar como fomos perdoados

Por fim, ele descreve o perdão como uma promessa: não vou mais usar esse pecado contra você, não vou ficar remoendo, não vou espalhá-lo e não vou deixar que ele fique entre nós. Esse perdão nasce de lembrar o quanto Cristo nos perdoou. Em situações de abuso ou violência, porém, a prioridade é a segurança, e a reconciliação exige arrependimento demonstrado.

Na próxima discussão com seu cônjuge, faça uma pausa e pergunte a si mesmo: qual é a minha parte nisso? Confesse primeiro, com palavras claras. Leia Efésios 4:29-32 juntos e orem pedindo um coração perdoador.

items.title: Um casamento que conta o evangelho
items.author: Ray Ortlund
items.work: Marriage and the Mystery of the Gospel (2016)
items.body:
Ray Ortlund, pastor e estudioso do Antigo Testamento, escreveu um livro curto que percorre a Bíblia do começo ao fim para mostrar o que Deus pensa do casamento. Sua conclusão é que o casamento não é apenas um arranjo útil para a sociedade, mas uma imagem viva do amor de Cristo pela igreja.

## Desde o jardim

Ortlund começa em Gênesis. Deus cria o homem e a mulher, os une e declara que se tornam uma só carne. Há ali alegria, companheirismo e ausência de vergonha. O pecado traz acusação, esconderijo e conflito. Desde então, os casais vivem entre a beleza do plano de Deus e as marcas da queda.

## Deus como marido fiel

No Antigo Testamento, os profetas descrevem Deus como um marido fiel e Israel como uma esposa que se desvia. Oseias é chamado a amar uma mulher infiel como sinal do amor do Senhor. Ortlund mostra que essas imagens revelam um Deus que não desiste do seu povo. O casamento humano aprende com esse amor persistente.

## O mistério revelado

Em Efésios 5, Paulo diz que o casamento é um grande mistério, e que ele está falando de Cristo e da igreja. Ortlund explica que o marido é chamado a amar como Cristo, que se entregou; a esposa é chamada a responder com respeito e confiança, como a igreja responde a Cristo. Isso não se trata de superioridade, mas de dois papéis que, juntos, contam uma história maior.

## Esperança para casais reais

Ortlund lembra que nenhum casamento retrata perfeitamente essa história. Mas Cristo é o noivo perfeito que cobre as nossas falhas. Por isso os casais podem recomeçar, pedir perdão e crescer, sabendo que caminham para as bodas do Cordeiro.

Leia Efésios 5:22-33 com seu cônjuge nesta semana. Cada um escolha uma atitude concreta para refletir melhor o amor de Cristo no outro, e orem juntos pedindo graça para viver assim.
